note: the one reading of a stored origin down to its host name, and the rows the two implementations of it must agree on: hostOf and hostsOf in packages/operator/src/origins.ts, and Hosts in packages/console/internal/widget/widget.go. one file and not one per language, because a second copy of these rows is the duplication the gate exists to catch, arrived at one level up. json rather than a module so the go module can read it: it has no package.json and reaches no workspace package, so it opens this file by path (packages/console/internal/widget/widget_test.go) where the typescript half imports it.
rows-note: each row is one stored origin and the host it must read to, null where the row is dropped. read in order the whole list is also the list reading: first-seen order kept, repeats out, dropped rows gone. every host here is lowercase and punycoded already, because a site is stored as URL.origin — that is a property of the storage path and of neither function, and it is pinned here so a store that stopped normalising cannot quietly move what reaches them.

rows.why: a stored origin may carry a port, and nothing that takes a host name takes one on the end of it.
the ordinary row, lowercase and unpunycoded because URL.origin made it so before it was stored.
an internationalised name arrives already punycoded, for the same reason, and neither implementation encodes one itself.
bare, without the brackets url.hostname hands back: a dev server binding v6-first sends exactly this origin, and both lists become a vendor's domain field, which takes a host name and not url syntax.
a row an operator added and never filled in is a value with no host in it, dropped rather than passed through.
no address in it at all, and not an error to either reader: a list is what they are handed.
a scheme with no authority after it parses on both sides and holds no host.
the same host as the second row: two stored origins are one domain, so the list reading keeps the first and drops this one.
